- EKC: emissions rise early growth, fall later; validity: country income, sector mix, energy policy.
* Environmental Kuznets Curve: inverted-U supported high-income economies; weaker/flat low/middle income, driven technology, regulation, scale effects.
- Structural breaks matter; crisis, reforms, energy prices shift trajectory.
* Growth-accounting evidence: energy intensity, carbon intensity, factor productivity, investment, trade openness, education influence emissions trajectory.
- High productivity, green innovation enable GDP decoupling, CO2 decline; dirty capital stock locks emissions.

- Results sensitivity: endogeneity, nonstationarity, lag order, country heterogeneity, unit-root errors.
* Policy implications: carbon pricing, renewable subsidies, industrial modernization, transport electrification, efficiency standards reduce marginal carbon intensity.
- Fiscal/monetary coordination needed; abrupt controls risk growth slowdown; gradual transitions support stable employment.
* Data limitations: national totals, sectoral aggregation, missing renewable/circular-economy indicators, short windows, inconsistent definitions.
- Future work: subnational panels, high-frequency electricity data, structural modeling, uncertainty quantification, policy counterfactuals.
